content: In school dental screening programs, dental health professionals conduct visual inspections of children’s oral cavities within the school environment. They then provide parents with information regarding their child’s current oral health status and any treatment needs. The primary goal of these programs is to identify potential oral health issues before they become symptomatic, thereby encouraging preventive and therapeutic care for children. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of school dental screening programs in improving oral health outcomes and increasing the use of dental services. It represents the second update of a review initially published in December 2017, with the first update completed in August 2019. To gather evidence, an information specialist conducted a search of four bibliographic databases up to October 15, 2021, and employed additional methods to identify both published and unpublished studies, as well as ongoing research. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), either clusteror individually randomized, that compared school dental screening to no intervention or compared different types of screening approaches. The updated review incorporated eight trials, including six cluster-RCTs, involving a total of 21,290 children aged 4 to 15 years. Four of these trials were conducted in the UK, two in India, one in the USA, and one in Saudi Arabia. Among these, two trials were assessed as having a low risk of bias, three as having a high risk of bias, and three as having an unclear risk of bias. None of the trials included long-term follow-up to evaluate the sustained effects of school dental screening, with outcomes assessed only at 3 to 11 months post-intervention. The trials did not report on the proportion of children with treated or untreated oral diseases other than dental caries. Additionally, no data were provided on the cost-effectiveness of the programs or any potential adverse events associated with them. Four trials compared traditional school dental screening to no screening. A meta-analysis was conducted to assess the outcome of dental attendance, but the results were inconclusive due to high heterogeneity among the studies. This heterogeneity was partly attributed to differences in study design, as three trials were cluster-RCTs and one was individually randomized. Due to this inconsistency and the unclear risk of bias, the evidence was downgraded to very low certainty, making it impossible to draw definitive conclusions about this comparison. Two cluster-RCTs, both involving four-arm designs, evaluated criteria-based screening compared to no screening. The findings suggested a potential small benefit in dental attendance (pooled risk ratio [RR] 1.07, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.99 to 1.16; low-certainty evidence). However, when criteria-based screening was compared to traditional screening, no significant difference was observed (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.08; very low-certainty evidence). One trial investigated the use of a specific (personalized) referral letter compared to a non-specific referral letter. The results indicated that specific referral letters were more effective in increasing attendance at general dental services (RR 1.39, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.77; very low-certainty evidence) and specialist orthodontic services (RR 1.90, 95% CI 1.18 to 3.06; very low-certainty evidence). Another trial compared screening supplemented with motivational interventions (such as oral health education and offers of free treatment) to screening alone. The findings suggested that dental attendance was more likely when motivation was included (RR 3.08, 95% CI 2.57 to 3.71; very low-certainty evidence). One trial compared referrals to a specific dental treatment facility with general advice to visit a dentist. No significant difference in dental attendance was observed between these two referral methods (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.34 to 2.47; very low-certainty evidence). Only one trial reported on the proportion of children with treated dental caries. This trial evaluated a referral letter based on the common-sense model of self-regulation (a theoretical framework explaining how individuals perceive and respond to health threats), with or without an accompanying dental information guide, compared to a standard referral letter. The findings were inconclusive, and the evidence was assessed as very low certainty due to high risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision. In conclusion, the evidence is insufficient to determine whether school dental screening programs improve dental attendance or oral health outcomes. It remains uncertain whether traditional screening is more effective than no screening (very low-certainty evidence). Criteria-based screening may offer a slight improvement in dental attendance compared to no screening (low-certainty evidence), but no difference was observed when compared to traditional screening (very low-certainty evidence). Personalized referral letters may improve dental attendance compared to non-specific letters (very low-certainty evidence). Screening supplemented with motivational interventions may also enhance dental attendance compared to screening alone (very low-certainty evidence). However, it is unclear whether referral letters based on the common-sense model of self-regulation are more effective than standard referral letters, or whether specific referrals to dental treatment facilities are superior to general advice to visit a dentist (very low-certainty evidence). The trials included in this review primarily evaluated the short-term effects of school dental screening programs. None of the studies assessed their long-term effectiveness in improving oral health, nor did they address potential adverse effects or cost implications.
